sections.title: Mission · Turn Commands into Automation
paragraphs: This is the heaviest objective in World 3. You already know individual commands; now learn how repetitive commands become a script—a sequence of instructions the computer executes for you.

sections.title: What Is a Shell Script?
paragraphs: A shell script is a text file containing commands intended for a shell. Instead of typing echo Starting, date, and echo Finished every time, save the sequence in a script.
sections.callout: A SCRIPT IS THE BEGINNING OF AUTOMATION

sections.title: Why Script?
paragraphs: Scripts support repetitive tasks, consistent operations, automation, administration, reduced manual typing, and command workflows.
sections.callout: IF YOU REPEATEDLY PERFORM THE SAME COMMAND SEQUENCE, AUTOMATE IT

sections.title: Text Editors
paragraphs: Scripts are plain-text files, so you need a text editor to create or modify them. This objective specifically requires awareness of vi and nano.

sections.title: vi
paragraphs: vi is a traditional Unix and Linux text editor. It is modal: command mode interprets keys as editing commands, while insert mode enters text. Linux Essentials requires recognition of this basic model, not mastery of every vi command.
sections.callout: vi = MODAL TEXT EDITOR · COMMAND MODE + INSERT MODE

sections.title: nano
paragraphs: nano is a command-line text editor often considered easier for beginners. It displays common keyboard shortcuts along the bottom of its interface, so basic actions remain visible while editing. Need to edit a shell script from the terminal? vi or nano.
sections.callout: nano = VISIBLE SHORTCUTS · BEGINNER-FRIENDLY TERMINAL EDITOR

sections.title: The Shebang
paragraphs: A script can begin with #!, called the shebang. A common Bash script begins with #!/bin/bash, telling the system which interpreter should execute it.

sections.title: /bin/bash
paragraphs: In #!/bin/bash, /bin/bash identifies Bash as the interpreter.

sections.title: Exam Trap · Shebang
paragraphs: At the beginning of a script, #! is the interpreter directive. It is not merely a comment, filename, variable, or loop.

sections.title: A Simple Script
paragraphs: A conceptual script can begin with #!/bin/bash and then run echo "Welcome to GSA". Bash processes the file and echo displays the message. Scripting saves commands instead of requiring you to enter them manually every time.
sections.callout: THE SHELL RUNS THE SAVED COMMANDS IN SEQUENCE

sections.title: Variables in Scripts
paragraphs: Variables store values inside scripts. academy="GSA" followed by echo "$academy" displays GSA. Variables make scripts reusable and flexible.

sections.title: Arguments
paragraphs: Scripts can receive command-line arguments. If ./hello.sh Edelmiro is invoked, the script can access supplied values with positional parameters such as $1, $2, and $3.

sections.title: Script Name and Arguments
paragraphs: With ./hello.sh Linux, echo "$1" can display Linux.
sections.callout: $0 = ME · $1 = FIRST THING GIVEN TO ME · $2 = SECOND

sections.title: Why Arguments Matter
paragraphs: Arguments let one script accept different input. ./backup.sh Documents and ./backup.sh Projects can reuse the same script with different targets.

sections.title: for Loops
paragraphs: A loop repeats instructions. In a conceptual for name in John Maria David; do echo "$name"; done sequence, the command runs once for each name.
sections.callout: FOR = DO THIS FOR EACH ITEM

sections.title: Understanding the Loop
paragraphs: In for name in John Maria David, name receives each value in turn. do begins the commands to repeat, and done ends the loop.

sections.title: Why Loops Matter
paragraphs: If ten files need the same operation, a loop replaces ten manual repetitions. This is a foundation of automation.

sections.title: echo in Scripts
paragraphs: echo displays messages and variables, shows progress, and produces output. echo "Backup starting" tells the user what the script is doing.
sections.callout: A SCRIPT DOES NOT NEED TO OPERATE SILENTLY

sections.title: Commands Have Results
paragraphs: When a Linux command finishes, it returns an exit status indicating success or a problem. Zero means success; nonzero means some kind of failure or other condition.

sections.title: $? · The Previous Exit Status
paragraphs: The special shell variable $? contains the exit status of the most recently executed command. After running a command, echo $? displays that result.
sections.callout: $? = HOW DID THE LAST COMMAND DO?

sections.title: Exam Trap · Exit Status
paragraphs: Do not assume 1 is good and 0 is bad. Shell exit-status convention is 0 for success and nonzero for not-success or another condition.

sections.title: Scripts Can Make Decisions from Results
paragraphs: A script can run a command, receive its status, inspect the result, and react. This is a major foundation of automation.

sections.title: Putting the Pieces Together
paragraphs: #!/bin/bash, name="$1", and echo "Welcome, $name" combine a shebang, Bash, an argument, a variable, quoting, and echo. A for item in one two three loop combines a variable with a repeated command.

sections.title: The GSA Automation Connection
paragraphs: Earlier objectives taught you to navigate, create files, list files, search, and archive. A script can combine those commands.

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Save repetitive commands for reuse → Shell script
Edit a script in the terminal → vi or nano
Receive a value after the script filename → Argument
Repeat commands for several items → for loop
Know whether the previous command succeeded → Exit status or $?
sections.callout: SCRIPT · EDITOR · INTERPRETER · VARIABLE · ARGUMENT · LOOP · OUTPUT · STATUS

sections.title: GSA Exam Traps

entries.title: Shebang vs. Comment
paragraphs: #!/bin/bash is an interpreter directive at the beginning of a script.

entries.title: Variable vs. Argument
paragraphs: A variable stores a value. An argument is supplied when invoking a command or script.

entries.title: $1 vs. $?
paragraphs: $1 is the first positional argument. $? is the previous command's exit status.

entries.title: Exit Status
paragraphs: 0 is success. Nonzero is failure or another condition.

entries.title: vi vs. nano
paragraphs: Both are text editors, not shells. vi is recognized by command and insert modes; nano displays common shortcuts on screen.

sections.callout: READ THE SYMBOL AND ITS CONTEXT PRECISELY

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: vi → Modal editor with command and insert modes
nano → Editor with visible shortcut reminders
